 Search Program: Call that a heatwave? Why a heatwave in Tasmania is different to one in Queensland 
 Source: 936 ABC Hobart | Program: Tasmania Afternoons 
 Wed 21 Oct 2026 at 1:30pm Wed 21 Oct 2026 at 1:30pm Wed 21 Oct 2026 at 1:30pm Space to play or pause, M to mute, left and right arrows to seek, up and down arrows for volume. Play   Duration: 6 minutes 10 seconds 6 m Brought to you by
 936 ABC Hobart Presented by
 Kylie Baxter The Bureau of Meteorology has issued a low-to-severe heatwave warning for much of southern and eastern Tasmania from Wednesday 21 to Friday 23 October.
 Every time a heatwave warning is mentioned on 936 ABC Radio and ABC Northern Tasmania, the text messages start to flood in about it not being hot enough to be called a heatwave.
 So Kylie Baxter on Tasmania Afternoons asks an expert, Angus Hines, senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, to explain what the thresholds are in Tasmania for a few warm days to be called a heatwave and why it matters.
 Credits
 Kylie Baxter, Presenter 
 Lucy Bain, Producer 
 Image Details
 A low-to-severe heatwave has been declared for much of Tasmania for 21 October to 23 October, 2026.
 ( ABC News: Laura Beavis ) 
 Program: More from Tasmania Afternoons Hobart, Launceston, Weather Warnings Transcript 
 Kylie Baxter 
But how do you decide to call it a heatwave? What are the trigger points?
 Angus Hines 
Yeah, look, that is a great question. And I think the key thing is a heatwave is defined as three consecutive days. So three consecutive days and actually the three consecutive nights in between them where the temperatures recorded are significantly above average for that location. And because of that location thing, it means that the heatwave threshold is actually different depending on where you look in the country. So areas which typically average cooler temperatures have got a cooler threshold to reach before they'll be classified as a heatwave. But warmer parts of the country have to get to a much higher temperature before a heatwave is declared in some of those areas. So it's three days and nights in a row can be longer than that, but it can't be shorter than that. So one hot day, no matter how hot it is, won't classify as a heatwave. But once we get to three days or more where those temperatures are staying above average through the day and really importantly through the night as well, because if it's a hot day or let's say three hot days in a row, but we've got still clear nights where the temperature really plunges overnight, which can happen in certain weather situations, that won't be a heatwave because generally people's bodies are able to recover through the night if it really cools off. But if it's those night-time temperatures are also mild and maybe it's a little bit difficult to sleep, you can't quite shake the heat of the day, then that's when those heatwave warnings get issued.
 Kylie Baxter 
You can probably understand why some people find it confusing to get heatwave warnings when it's actually not that hot. Like, for example, right now, it doesn't feel all that hot. I mean, it's warmer in Launceston, but it is confusing for people. Can you accept that?
 Angus Hines 
Yeah, I mean, it can be a little bit confusing. I think there's maybe a few other things to keep in mind, I suppose, with the heatwave warnings. So we've got we've got different severity for our heatwave warnings and large parts of Tasmania have qualified for or reached the threshold for what we call a low intensity heatwave, which is the lowest of those thresholds that get reached. So that's now, is it? Well, that's for large parts of the state, not absolutely everywhere, but many areas in the south and the east of the state are in those low intensity heatwave conditions. There are a few pockets of the state which are in the next tier up, which is called severe heatwave, where those temperatures are a little bit higher away from average. And for those low intensity heatwaves in particular, it's a common part of the the warm time of year for Australia. They happen pretty regularly. And we expect that most people can cope pretty, pretty handily with a low intensity heatwave. It's not going to have too much of an impact on most people who are, you know, healthy and not spending their full day out in the sunshine. But some people are affected by heatwaves a little bit more severely than others. So we tend to make sure that we're including the message in there for people who are maybe already a bit sick or perhaps the elderly who tend to get hit a little bit harder by heatwaves, even if, you know, the majority of the population is not too much to worry about.
 Kylie Baxter 
And is the threshold different in Tasmania compared to, say, Queensland, Northern Territory, Western Australia?
 Angus Hines 
Yeah, it absolutely is. The threshold that is set for those heatwaves is related to the average temperature that each location experiences throughout the course of the year. So Hobart and Tasmania as a whole, on average, living in a cooler climate, have got lower maximum temperatures and minimum temperatures required before we're starting to push into those heatwave thresholds. Whereas you go to much warmer places up in the north and west where the average temperature is much higher, then those temperatures have to really overshoot their average by about the same margin in order before we'll be talking about heatwaves in those parts of the country. So the thresholds vary quite significantly around the country. And that's because Australia has just got such a varied climate. Different parts of the country and different parts even within the same state have such different average conditions that they experience over a summer that there's just no one size fits all heatwave threshold that you could apply to the country that would make sense.
 Kylie Baxter 
This texter, Barney's in Richmond and says, Kylie, it's an absolute joke to declare a heatwave when temperatures are in the 20s and low 30s. It's meaningless to many people and takes away confidence in the Bureau. Another texter, Sue in Penna says a heatwave, what nonsense, two hot days tomorrow and then Saturday and Sunday will be a lot lower in her area. She says only around 15 degrees. And another one, weather's OK near Swansea, there's no heatwave and it doesn't seem to be that hot in the coming days. You can see how for a lot of people it's driving them mad.
 Angus Hines 
Yeah, well, the text there that talked about the weekend, there's certainly not going to still be heatwave warnings continuing through the weekend when those temperatures do drop 10 or 15 degrees. I'll just add one more thing into the mix when it comes to that that heatwave threshold that we talked about earlier. It is a little bit of a complex equation, but there's actually an element in that equation which relates to recent conditions. So it takes into account the temperatures over the last 30 days when factoring in whether or not we declare this as a heatwave or not. And that's because if it has been relatively cool, when you do see those temperatures spike, that can be a bit of a shock to the system and perhaps more so than towards the end of summer when we might have had two, three, four, five spells of heat and then we get another one. That's not going to be such a shock when you're a little bit more acclimatised to that hot weather. So I think part of the heatwave flagging this week is that we're in spring, which means we're coming on the back of some much cooler weather, really, through the end of winter, the start of spring. And the temperatures in those last 30 days have been nothing especially unusual. We've had the odd warm day here and there. But seeing these multiple 30 degree days, it is a real shift in what we've seen recently. It's a real notable jump compared to recent conditions over the last month or so. So if we were to, you know, copy and paste the temperatures this week to a week in the middle of February, when we'd just gone through, you know, a long and potentially hot summer, then we wouldn't have that same adjustment compared to recent conditions. And perhaps the same temperatures that we're experiencing now wouldn't necessarily qualify as a heatwave in the middle of summer. So that's an element to it as well. This hot spell is especially hot because it hasn't been that warm recently.
